title: AI in Schools: Three Things to Get Right
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick argues that most school AI policies are compliance-heavy documents focused on safeguarding and data protection while offering little real guidance on curriculum, instruction, and assessment. Drawing on Ethan Mollick's framing of AI as a fast-diffusing "general purpose technology," he lays out three things school leaders need to get right. First, curriculum planning needs genuine disciplinary expertise, since AI systems struggle to distinguish procedural from declarative knowledge and can produce curricula that look convincing but lack real conceptual structure. Second, adaptive learning must move beyond simple difficulty adjustment toward systems that diagnose why a student is struggling, not just whether their answer was right or wrong. Third, human judgement must stay central to assessment, illustrated by Daisy Christodoulou's comparative-judgement model, where AI handles the logistics of marking but teachers retain the actual judgement. Hendrick closes by framing AI policy as a living, evolving document rather than a one-time compliance exercise.
points: Hendrick's central metaphor is the "plastic plant" curriculum -- AI-generated curricula that look convincing on the surface but lack the roots and depth that expert teachers build into real curriculum design.

His policy recommendation is structural: subject-specific curriculum teams, not IT departments, should lead AI procurement decisions, because the right question is whether a tool understands a subject the way the best teachers do.

On adaptive learning, he argues most edtech "adaptivity" has historically meant difficulty adjustment, not genuine diagnostic responsiveness -- and that AI's pattern-matching over large datasets could finally close that gap if designed around real diagnostic insight rather than engagement metrics.

The comparative-judgement example (Daisy Christodoulou / No More Marking) shows Hendrick's preferred model for AI and assessment: AI accelerates the logistics of marking, but the actual judgement stays with the teacher.
quotes: AI is best understood as a “General Purpose Technology”, akin to steam power, electricity, or the internet, except it is unfolding at a much faster pace and at the level of cognition rather than mechanics.

I get the sense that ahead of the new school year, some schools are working with AI-generated curricula which are effectively plastic plants: they may look convincing on the surface but lack the roots, depth, and vitality of real curricula developed by expert teachers.

Schools need subject specific curriculum teams, not just IT departments, leading AI procurement decisions. The key question isn't "Does this AI system work?" but "Does it understand our subject the way our best teachers do?
Many of these personalised systems have tracked right/wrong answers but then failed to capture why a student is struggling and more importantly, what to do about it.
This keeps teachers as the arbiters of quality while AI handles the legwork, delivering comparable scores and feedback with far less time than traditional marking.
As Dylan Wiliam recently cautioned, AI tools may help with logistics like scoring or collating, but “there are limitations to AI's feedback and assessment capabilities”.
